## Declarations and implementations

```plato
//==
// # Algebra
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Magnitude, distance, and order-lattice interfaces
//  - Numeric tower interfaces
//  - Algebraic operation interfaces

//==
// # Magnitude, distance, and order-lattice interfaces
//
// The geometric half of the algebra vocabulary: length, distance, component-wise
// extrema and clamping, and the affine point/delta relationship.

// Has a notion of length or magnitude (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_(mathematics)).
// MagnitudeSquared avoids the square root when only relative comparisons are needed.
interface INormed
{
    Magnitude(x: Self): Number;
    MagnitudeSquared(x: Self): Number;
}

// A space with a distance between any two of its values. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)
interface IMetricSpace
{
    Distance(a: Self, b: Self): Number;
}

// Supports component-wise minimum and maximum: a lattice. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(order))
interface ILattice
{
    Min(a: Self, b: Self): Self;
    Max(a: Self, b: Self): Self;
}

// Can be clamped to lie within inclusive bounds. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clamping_(graphics))
interface IClampable
    inherits ILattice
{
    Clamp(x: Self, min: Self, max: Self): Self;
}

// A position-like type whose difference is a separate delta type: subtracting two
// points yields a vector; adding a vector to a point yields a point.
// See affine space (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_space).
//
// TDelta is bound to IAdditive and Scalable: the deltas are the group acting on
// the positions, so they must at least add, negate, and scale. Every delta in
// this vocabulary already satisfies both (Vector2D/3D/N via INumerical, Duration
// via IQuantity), and the bound is what lets the rest of the affine surface —
// Subtract in both spellings, Lerp, and the reversed Add — be derived once in
// algebra.library.plato instead of hand-written per implementor.
//
// Only two members are primitive. Add and Between are exactly the torsor action
// and its inverse; everything else in the affine API follows from them.
interface IDifference<TDelta>
    where TDelta: IAdditive, TDelta: IScalable
{
    Add(x: Self, delta: TDelta): Self;
    // The displacement FROM a TO b, i.e. b - a. Direction convention: Between and
    // Add are inverse, so a.Add(a.Between(b)) == b. Every implementor and every
    // caller relies on this orientation (Point2D/Point3D honor it in
    // transforms.library.plato; the ScaleAbout/RotateAbout helpers in
    // intervals-transforms-deformable.library.plato assume it).
    Between(a: Self, b: Self): TDelta;
}

// An affine position measured as a displacement from a distinguished origin.
// Fixing an origin makes the position space and its delta space interchangeable
// (in the language of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsor, a trivialized
// torsor), which is what lets Add and Between themselves be derived rather than
// declared: an implementing type owes only the two conversions below.
//
// A Point's origin is (0, 0[, 0]); an Instant's is its epoch. Both were already
// spelling these conversions by hand under other names — PositionVector/ToPoint
// on the point types, SecondsSinceEpoch on Instant.
//
// This is deliberately OPTIONAL and deliberately a SUBTYPE. Optional, because a
// position type whose delta conversion is not a cheap relabeling — a homogeneous
// point, where recovering the Cartesian delta needs a divide by W — implements
// `IDifference` directly and writes Add/Between itself. A subtype, so that a type
// declares one interface rather than two and cannot claim the conversions while
// forgetting the affine API they serve.
interface IOriginBased<TDelta>
    inherits IDifference<TDelta>
{
    // The displacement of this position from the origin.
    Offset(x: Self): TDelta;
    // The position at the given displacement from the origin. The receiver only
    // selects the type (and, for runtime-arity positions, the arity).
    FromOffset(_: Self, d: TDelta): Self;
}

//==
// # Numeric tower interfaces
//
// The number-like family, from representable limits up through the reals and the
// whole numbers. Each level adds capability to the level below; Number and
// Integer are the canonical instances of IReal and IWhole.

// Has a distinguished one element and representable extremes. The additive
// identity is NOT here: Zero is a property of the additive group and lives on
// `IAdditive` (algebra.concepts.plato), which every INumerical also
// inherits — so a INumerical still reaches Zero, while a IQuantity or IMatrix
// gets it without having to claim representable extremes it has no meaning for.
interface INumericalLimits
{
    One(x: Self): Self;
    MinValue(x: Self): Self;
    MaxValue(x: Self): Self;
}

// The family of number-like value types: additive, scalable, interpolatable,
// with known limits. Includes reals, complex numbers, vectors, and quantities.
interface INumerical
    inherits IValue, IAdditive, IScalable, IInterpolatable, INumericalLimits
{ }

// A continuous one-dimensional number with full arithmetic and total order.
// Number is the canonical instance. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)
interface IReal
    inherits INumerical, IComparable, IHashable, IArithmetic, IInvertible
{
    ToNumber(x: Self): Number;

    // The non-negative square root (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root). Precondition: x is not negative.
    Sqrt(x: Self): Self;
    // Floor and ceiling (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions):
    // The largest whole value less than or equal to x.
    Floor(x: Self): Self;
    // The smallest whole value greater than or equal to x.
    Ceiling(x: Self): Self;
}

// IWhole-number semantics: exact, ordered, arithmetic without a multiplicative
// inverse (division truncates). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)
interface IWhole
    inherits IValue, IComparable, IHashable, IArithmetic, IInterpolatable, INumericalLimits
{
    ToInteger(x: Self): Integer;
}
```
